p06hps8.editorialNote:
This is not considered a definitive periodization of the archaeology of Ireland, but rather a tool to be developed for the standardisation across heritage inventories that cover the island of Ireland, and the C14 project undertaken by University College Dublin. Temporal boundaries have not been taken from any one source. Each of the Irish partners has provided a list of boundaries used in their inventories. These have been collated to come up with generic boundaries.

The periods list is used to reconcile named periods to date ranges in the ARIADNEplus project

p08m57h54j8.label: Indus Civilisation
p08m57h54j8.note: Urban civilisation based in the northwestern part of the Indian subcontinent, today in Pakistan and western India.  Developing out of earlier prehistoric cultures, it flourished over a very wide area between approximately 2,500 and 2,000 BC.  Script was known but is undeciphered today, not least as surviving inscriptions (mostly on seals) are no more than about a dozen characters.  Major settlements, such as Mohenjo-daro and Harappa, were laid out on a grid pattern with drainage and were clearly organised by a central power.  The earliest fragments of woven cotton from the subcontinent come from these sites.  Trade with sites in the Persian Gulf, as well as with settlements on the Oxus, has been substantiated.

p0kh9ds.editorialNote:
Historic England Periods is a key guide for dating Britain's historic sites and monuments. The list is made available via the Forum on Information Standards in Heritage (FISH - see https://heritage-standards.org.uk/chronology/). The data has subsequently been converted to SKOS RDF format and published as Linked Open Data at http://purl.org/heritagedata/schemes/eh_period
Two significant updates to the originally published list (May 2024 and February 2026) have been reflected in this dataset.

p0kh9ds7q8m.editorialNote: September 2024 - revisions to reflect latest data as published May 2024
p0kh9ds7q8m.label: Bronze Age
p0kh9ds7q8m.note: This period follows on from the Neolithic and is characterized by the increasing use of Bronzework. It is subdivided in the Early, Middle and Late Bronze Age. Circa -2600 BCE to -700 BCE.

p0kh9dsbz2g.editorialNote: September 2024 - revisions to reflect latest data as published May 2024
p0kh9dsbz2g.label: Neolithic
p0kh9dsbz2g.note: The New Stone Age, this period follows on from the Palaeolithic and the Mesolithic and is itself succeeded by the Bronze Age. This period is characterized by the practice of a farming economy and extensive monumental constructions. Circa -4000 BCE to -2200 BCE.

p0kh9dsj33x.editorialNote: September 2024 - revisions to reflect latest data as published May 2024
p0kh9dsj33x.label: Iron Age
p0kh9dsj33x.note: This period follows on from the Bronze Age and is characterized by the use of iron for making tools and monuments such as hillforts and oppida. The Iron Age is taken to end with the Roman invasion. Circa -800 BCE to 43 CE.

p0kh9dskb4p.editorialNote: September 2024 - new period to reflect latest data as published May 2024
p0kh9dskb4p.label: Chalcolithic
p0kh9dskb4p.note: The transitional period at the end of the Neolithic when metal is first used to make tools and weapons. New burial rites and artefacts appear at the same time as these copper implements appear. Circa -2500 BCE to -2200 BCE.

p0s2rwk.editorialNote:
Andrew Kandel who has provided the period data is a member of the team undertaking the The Role of Culture in Early Expansions of Humans (ROCEEH) project. The data originates from the ROCEEH Out of Africa Database (ROAD). Sarah Wurz provided the Afrikaans period labels.

ROCEEH deals with the time from ca. 3 million to 20,000 before present. The periods in this authority reflect accepted cultural entities, which ROCEEH calls ArchStrats. The age ranges are approximate and based on publications and ROCEEH's own interpretations.

p0s2rwkchqc.label: Middle Paleolithic
p0s2rwkchqc.note:
Sites with prepared core technologies.

The age range is very broad and based on the maximum age for Attirampakkam and the minimum age for Jwalapuram, both in southern India. Together these define the MP of India, which tends to overlap with dates of the LP.

p0s2rwkgzwv.editorialNote: Date range adjusted as of June 2024.
p0s2rwkgzwv.label: Lower Paleolithic
p0s2rwkgzwv.note: General LP techno-complexes from S Asia, with ages parallel to the Acheulean. However, there is no clear distinction between those two technocomplexes. Thus far, there is no evidence for pre-Acheulean cultures in South Asia.

p0s2rwkj4cn.label: Upper Paleolithic
p0s2rwkj4cn.note:
Sites with undefined Upper Paleolithic technologies, usually includes laminar debitage but not microliths.

Age range based on max age for microlithic industries and general min age for Pleistocene.

p0s2rwkkkxz.label: Neolithic
p0s2rwkkkxz.note: Early farming societies, dates based on early start in Levant and late end in Europe.

p0s2rwkn8cc.label: Aurignacian
p0s2rwkn8cc.note: General Aurignacian techno-complexes from Europe with carinated tools, blade industry, bone tools, figurative art.

p0s2rwkp552.label: Lower Paleolithic
p0s2rwkp552.note: General Lower Paleolithic with no further details.

p0s2rwkp72n.label: Solutrean
p0s2rwkp72n.note:
Different bifacially retouched tool types, especially leaf points.

Includes Solutrean and also Badegoulian industries.

p0s2rwkrbhq.label: Iron Age
p0s2rwkrbhq.note: Farming societies, agriculturalists with metal, animals, farming, generally defined

p0s2rwkrjbs.editorialNote: Added per request of ROCEEH-ROAD data manager.
p0s2rwkrjbs.label: Paleolithic
p0s2rwkrjbs.note: "Generic Paleolithic" period definition not used to describe ROCEEH-ROAD data, but added to authority in order to align ROCEEH dataset properly with ARIADNE.

p0s2rwkrm8q.label: Kebaran
p0s2rwkrm8q.note:
Simple, lacks complexity and abundance of forms compared to later industries. Differences fluid, assemblages dominated by micropoints (curved backed bladelets with wider base), backed points, obliquely truncated backed bladelets, micropoints, or other backed pieces. Summary: No habitual use of the microburin technique, Mostly non-geometric microliths, First industry with invasive retouch/backing of the pieces, Two large phases, with the later phase yielding truncated pieces.

Dates about 20-14 ka uncal BP Fellner (1995a, 22). A widespread phenomenon in the Mediterranean zone and oases of Palestine, Israel, southern Syria, Lebanon and western Jordan, extending into the desert areas of the Negev and Sinai. The desert areas seem to have been settled slightly later, with dates of about 16 ka uncal BP.

p0s2rwks8k2.label: Epipaleolithic
p0s2rwks8k2.note:
Late prehistoric hunter-gatherer societies before the advent of agriculture.

Technically, the Epipaleolithic is defined as the final phase of the Upper Paleolithic. However, we consider the Epipaleolithic as its own category because it falls mainly outside the time range and scope of the ROCEEH project.

p0s2rwksjfw.label: Natufian
p0s2rwksjfw.note:
Natufian most widely known Epipalaeolithic industry in Near East, already discovered in the 1920s. Ground stone tools and blades with sickle gloss indicate use and cultivation of cereals. Summary: Use of classical and Krukowski microburin technique, Lunates, size and style Helwan retouch or simple backing, Picks and sickle blades with gloss, Regular use of ground stone tools like mortars, mullers and pestles.

Natufian occurs in central and northern Palestine, with fewer finds in southern Palestine, the steppe of the Negev and Sinai, high Lebanon and Anti-Lebanon mountains, and Syro-Arabian Desert. Microliths and geometrics make up >40% of every assemblage.

p0s2rwkv3zf.label: Magdalenian
p0s2rwkv3zf.note: Blade-dominated industry, rich bone industry, figurative art, many different types of ornaments.

p0s2rwkwbsz.label: Bronze Age
p0s2rwkwbsz.note: Approximate beginning of the Bronze Age in Levant, through the beginning of the Iron Age in the Hittite Empire.

p0s2rwkwgnt.label: Mousterian
p0s2rwkwgnt.note: Based on Richter 2011, 2016 with focus on Marine Isotope Stage 8-3.

p0xxt6t.editorialNote:
Period data compiled as part of the ScAPA project and published as Linked Open Data. The ScAPA project was funded by Historic Environment Scotland, implemented by University of South Wales.
This dataset is based on the original compiled and published data, supplemented and revised according to more recent (May 2022) updates provided by HES.

p0xxt6tcq9w.label: Chalcolithic
p0xxt6tcq9w.note: The transitional period at the end of the Neolithic when metal is first used to make tools and weapons. New burial rites and artefacts appear at the same time as these copper implements appear.

p0xxt6tfv6h.label: Bronze Age
p0xxt6tfv6h.note: After the Neolithic and the first use of metal in the Chalcolithic, the Bronze Age is defined by advances in metal working to produce durable Bronze tools and weapons, accompanied by societal change. New architectural styles and burial practices appear.

p0xxt6tprqq.label: Neolithic
p0xxt6tprqq.note: The Neolithic, or New Stone Age, sees the transition from hunter gatherer economies to farming. Monumental architecture, including chambered cairns, develops. Pottery is first used and stone tool technologies become more sophisticated.

p0xxt6tvdbz.label: Iron Age
p0xxt6tvdbz.note: Tribal centres and elites appear in society at the end of the Bronze Age. There is a wide range of monumental buildings including brochs, duns and crannogs. Iron is used for tool making. The fall of Rome traditionally marks the end of the period.
